papers.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
papers.abstract: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

papers.title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
papers.abstract: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.

papers.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
papers.abstract: Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.

papers.title: Gray Codes With Constant Delay and Constant Auxiliary Space
papers.abstract: We give the first two algorithms to enumerate all binary words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ (like Gray codes) while ensuring that the delay and the auxiliary space is independent from $\ell$, i.e., constant time for each word, and constant memory in addition to the $\ell$ bits storing the current word. Our algorithms are given in two new computational models: tape machines and deque machines. We also study more restricted models, queue machines and stack machines, and show that they cannot enumerate all binary words with constant auxiliary space, even with unrestricted delay. A tape machine is a Turing machine that stores the current binary word on a single working tape of length $\ell$ (which never increases), using no other tape. The machine has a single head and must edit its tape to reach all possible words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$, and output them (in unit time, by entering special output states), with no duplicates. Hence a tape machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition (up to the head position). We construct a tape machine that achieves this task with constant delay between consecutive outputs, so that the machine implements a so-called skew-tolerant quasi-Gray code. We then construct a more involved tape machine that implements a Gray code. A deque machine stores the current binary word on a double-ended queue of length $\ell$, and stores a constant-size internal state. It works as a tape machine, except that it modifies the content of the deque by performing push and pop operations on the endpoints. Hence again a deque machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition. We construct deque machines that enumerate all words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ with constant-delay. The main technical challenge in this model is to correctly detect when enumeration has finished.

papers.title: Near-Optimal Online Metric Matching on $\Delta$-ary HST
papers.abstract: In the online metric matching problem, we have $n$ servers with known locations in some metric space. Requests arrive one-by-one at certain locations, and upon arrival a request must be matched to a server that was not matched to a previous request. The goal is to minimize the matching cost. For randomized algorithms with an oblivious adversary, the best known competitive ratio is obtained by embedding the metric space into an HST, and then solving the problem in the setting where the metric space is defined by the HST. Bansal et al. (Algorithmica, 2014) introduced a framework for online metric matching where one develops an algorithm in a restricted reassignment model, and then transforms this into a true online algorithm. Using this framework, they obtained an expected competitive ratio of $O(\log n)$ for HSTs; this also gives the best known competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 n)$ for general metrics. In this paper, we revisit this framework with the aim of developing new algorithms. For HSTs where each node has at most $\Delta$ children, we develop an algorithm via this framework with an expected competitive ratio of $O((\log\log \Delta) \cdot \log \Delta)$. In particular, this ratio is independent of $n$, the number of servers/requests. It is near-optimal, as the expected competitive ratio of any algorithm is $\Omega(\log \Delta)$.

papers.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
papers.abstract: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

papers.title: Online Tokenization with Optimal Delay in Linear Time
papers.abstract: Tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in almost all large language models (LLMs). One of the most popular frameworks is BPE tokenization, which consists of special token segmentation, pretokenization, and byte-pair encoding (BPE). However, existing algorithms are sequential, with each stage only processing complete output from the previous stage. In order to reduce latency and memory footprints, recent works (Jiang and Gong, ICML 2026) (Li, Yang and Mamouras, ASPLOS 2026) (Mamouras, Li and Yang, PLDI 2026) have initiated the study of online algorithms for subroutines such as pretokenization and BPE with a goal of streaming input to output as the input arrives online. However, the search for efficient online tokenization remains open. In this work, we formalize and resolve online tokenization. We introduce the notion of delay for online tokenization which characterizes the extent to which the algorithm output lags behind the (possibly computationally intractable) optimum. We give a near-linear time algorithm with optimal delay (up to constant factors). We complement this algorithm with a conditional lower bound: unless $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$, there is no polynomial time algorithm that beats the delay of our algorithm by more than a constant factor. We implement a practical variant for tokenizers from OpenAI's tiktoken and HuggingFace's tokenizers. We obtain a $7.9\times$-$34.8\times$ latency advantage (measured as time to first token) over tiktoken (as well as the recent gigatoken tokenizer) and our implementation maintains approximately constant memory usage independent of input size. Our implementation also achieves a $2.4\times$-$7.0\times$ improvement in throughput over tiktoken and $15.8\times$-$38.1\times$ over tokenizers.

papers.title: With Leverage, the Gambler is Not the One Who Gets Ruined
papers.abstract: In this note we explore the following simple question: How does the classic \emph{gambler's ruin} phenomenon change if we allow the gambler \emph{financial leverage}? We show that, with a moderate amount of leverage, it is possible for an (idealized) gambler to sustain seemingly improbable profits over a remarkably long time horizon without ever going bankrupt, \emph{even} if the gambler makes only fair bets. With a leverage ratio of $L = 10$ (less than what Lehman Brothers Holdings had from 1995--2008), the probability of multiplying one's money by $1000\times$ without going bankrupt is roughly $50\%$. More generally, given $L$-fold leverage, and given the goal of multiplying one's money by a factor of $r > 1$, the optimal gambling strategy has probability roughly $r^{-1/L}$ of success. The results in this note are designed as part of the course development for the CMU randomized algorithms course.

papers.title: Learning-Augmented Streaming Algorithms for Approximating Boolean Max-CSPs
papers.abstract: We study learning-augmented streaming algorithms for estimating the value of Boolean Maximum Constraint Satisfaction Problems (Max-CSPs). Specifically, we consider streaming algorithms equipped with an $\varepsilon$-accurate oracle: for each variable, the oracle outputs a label in $\{-1,1\}$ that agrees with a fixed optimal assignment with probability $1/2+\varepsilon$, and disagrees otherwise. Prior work by Dong, Peng, and Vakilian [ITCS 2025] showed that, for the special case of Max-Cut, such an oracle enables a $(1/2+\Omega(\varepsilon^2))$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams. We substantially generalize and strengthen their result, provided that a highly accurate estimate of $\varepsilon$ is available. For any Boolean Max-$2$CSP and any $\eta>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$, we obtain, with high constant probability, a single-pass $(1-\eta)$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/\eta)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/\eta,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams, where $n$ is the number of variables. We further extend our techniques to general Boolean Max-$k$CSPs for $k\ge 3$, with slightly worse space complexity.

papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Emergency Vertex Cover with Few Stations and Fault-Tolerant Coverage
papers.abstract: The Emergency Vertex Cover problem (Em-VC) assigns budgets to stations at graph vertices to cover every edge while minimizing the total budget. The cost of covering an edge from a station is the shortest-path distance from the station to the nearer endpoint plus the edge length. We study how restricting the number of stations affects the cost of ordinary and fault-tolerant coverage. In ordinary Em-VC, we prove that the optimal solution using at most two stations costs at most $5/4$ times the unrestricted optimum, improving the known $4/3$ guarantee for a single station. A recurrence extends this bound to larger station limits, giving approximation factors that converge to $\sqrt{5}-1$. Budget-threshold enumeration computes the restricted optimum in polynomial time for every fixed station limit. Under $k$-fold coverage, every edge must be covered by at least $k$ distinct stations, ensuring coverage after any $k-1$ station failures. We prove that selecting the $k$ vertices with the smallest full-coverage costs yields a $2$-approximation relative to the unrestricted optimum for $k$-fold coverage. When $k=2$, we combine upper bounds derived from the structure of the covering balls to improve the approximation guarantee to $5/3$.

papers.title: Revisiting Non-Adaptive Set Membership Schemes: Removing the Logarithmic Factor
papers.abstract: We study non-adaptive bit-probe schemes for static set membership. Each query reads a fixed number of bits and answers by strict majority. We revisit the random bipartite-graph construction of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017]. The main observation is that a slightly stronger expansion property already bounds the number of exceptional elements. This makes a separate probabilistic estimate for exceptional elements unnecessary. A detailed union-bound calculation then gives, for every fixed $t\ge5$, a logarithm-free existence bound of $O_t(m^{1/c}n^{1-1/c})$, where $c=\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor$. For odd $t$, this removes the logarithmic factor from the general upper bound of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017].

papers.title: Dynamic 3-Coloring of Bipartite Graphs with Optimal Locality
papers.abstract: We give a dynamic graph algorithm which maintains a 3-coloring in bipartite graphs under edge insertions such that the coloring only changes within a radius of $O(\log n)$ around an inserted edge. In the context of locality theory in distributed graph algorithms, this gives an upper bound on the locality under the dynamic-LOCAL model. Our bound on the locality is tight, as the problem admits a matching $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound in the stronger online-LOCAL model, by a result of Chang et al. [PODC 2024]. Thus, our result closes the gap between dynamic and online locality of this problem.

papers.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
papers.abstract: First defined by Bouchitt\'e and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimo\v{s}ov\'a, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013). Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitt\'e, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth. Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, {\em i.e.} a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.

papers.title: Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
papers.abstract: We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss. Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching. Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.

papers.title: Towards Dynamic Top-$k$ Simple Shortest Paths
papers.abstract: Computing the top-$k$ \textit{simple} shortest paths between two vertices of a graph, i.e., solving the P-KSSP problem, is a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. In modern scenarios, however, queries are rarely one-shot: parameters change as applications adapt their information needs, and recomputing a solution from scratch at every request quickly becomes a bottleneck. We study P-KSSP in a dynamic setting, focusing on changes of the parameter $k$: given a top-$k$ solution for a pair of vertices and a new value $k'$, the goal is to compute a top-$k'$ solution reusing the previously computed paths. Our approach rests on the \textit{pseudo-tree}, a compact representation of a collection of simple $s$--$t$ paths: we show that building it from an arbitrary, unstructured solution amounts to trie construction, and give two constructions running in time linear in the size of the collection. On top of it, we design UPD, a dynamic algorithm that updates a solution upon a change of $k$; we prove its correctness, analyze its complexity, and show that it is a general, solver-agnostic scheme, which starts from the paths alone, is parametric in the routine that generates candidate paths and combinable with known preprocessing techniques, as well as with an online pruning rule that we formalize. While a worst-case update is asymptotically comparable to recomputing from scratch, an extensive experimental evaluation shows that a variant of UPD is the fastest method in the large majority of tested configurations, often by a wide margin (with speedups over recomputation that grow with $k$ and $k'$ and exceed $60\times$), yielding a practical recipe for the configuration to deploy.

papers.title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
papers.abstract: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.

papers.title: Subexponential Parameterized Approximation for Group-Fair Euclidean $k$-Center
papers.abstract: Clustering is a basic tool for grouping data into meaningful classes, but in many applications the resulting clusters must also respect the fairness conditions among different groups. We study this direction for the group-fair Euclidean $k$-center problem in fixed dimension, where the input points are partitioned into disjoint color classes, and every cluster must satisfy given lower and upper bounds on the fraction of each color. We give a separator-based recursive approximation algorithm for the continuous-center setting. The main idea is to first reduce the continuous search space to a finite candidate center set and then use the geometric sphere separators to break the instance into smaller subproblems. Our algorithm gives a bicriteria approximation: the clustering radius is within a factor of $(1+\epsilon)$ of the optimum exactly fair solution, while the fairness bounds are relaxed only by a multiplicative factor. For fixed dimension, number of colors, and approximation parameters, the running time is polynomial in input size and subexponential in $k$. A recent IJCAI-ECAI2026 result gives a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for group-fair $k$-center in bounded doubling metrics with running time $(k/\epsilon)^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$. In the fixed-dimensional Euclidean setting considered here, we improve the dependence on $k$ to subexponential, while allowing continuous centers. The fairness guarantees of the two results are different: the previous work allows an additive fairness violation, whereas our algorithm uses a controlled multiplicative relaxation.

papers.title: Simple, Faster (min, +) Matrix Multiplication and APSP
papers.abstract: In this note, we provide a deterministic algorithm that computes the $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product $C = A * B$ of two $N \times N$ matrices $A$ and $B$ with polynomially bounded integer entries in $\tilde{O}(N^{2.9964})$ time, improving upon the exponent of $O(N^{2.9995})$ time obtained in the recent breakthrough by Anthropic (Alman and Vassilevska Williams, 2026). Our algorithm uses a phased approach first proposed by Bringmann, Grandoni, Saha, and Vassilevska Williams in 2016. The phased approach produces an approximation $\tilde{C}$ of $C$ in truly subcubic time such that the number of remaining triples $(i,k,j): A_{i,k}+B_{k,j} < \tilde{C}(i,j)$ is truly subcubic. This provided strong evidence that a truly subcubic $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product and therefore, a truly subcubic algorithm for All Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) may exist. However, to find the remaining triples in subcubic time, a sparse certificate is needed whose construction was not known. We use the thin matrix product theorem of the recent breakthrough to provide such a certificate. This gives a simple modular subcubic algorithm for APSP.

papers.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
papers.abstract: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ time, with probability at least $1-\delta$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.

papers.title: Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion Beyond Vertex Cover
papers.abstract: We study \textsc{Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion} (BDVD), where one asks whether at most \(k\) vertices can be deleted so that every remaining subgraph has density at most a rational input threshold \(\tau_\rho\). We address the twin-cover and distance-to-cluster cases left open by Raupach, Breitkopf, Herrmann, and Nichterlein (MFCS 2026). We prove fixed-parameter tractability parameterized solely by the twin-cover number, for unrestricted input density. For distance to cluster, we establish fixed-parameter tractability parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)+\lfloor2\tau_\rho+1\rfloor\), and complement this with \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hardness parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)\) alone when the target density is part of the input, even for integral targets. Thus distance to cluster alone is fixed-parameter tractable throughout \(\tau_\rho<1\), while it is insufficient for unrestricted input density. Finally, we settle the combined parameter treewidth plus solution size, an open problem posed by Bazgan, Nichterlein, and Vazquez Alferez (JCSS 2025). We prove that BDVD is \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hard parameterized by \(\operatorname{td}(G)+k\), and hence also by \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+k\), already for targets strictly between \(1\) and \(2\).

papers.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
papers.abstract: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

papers.title: A subquadratic upper bound for the mixing time of the Thorp shuffle
papers.abstract: Let $n=2^d$. We prove that the worst-start total-variation mixing time of the full labelled Thorp shuffle satisfies, for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1$, \[ t_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) \le C_* d^{5/3}+O_\varepsilon\!\left(d^{4/3}\log(d+2)\right), \qquad C_*=5.1536951454\ldots . \] Time is measured in ordinary Thorp shuffles. This improves the previously published full-deck upper bound $O(d^3)$ of Morris. The geometric starting point is elementary: label the $n=2^d$ positions by binary strings. One physical Thorp shuffle is a random swap layer on one coordinate matching of the $d$-dimensional cube, followed by a deterministic cyclic rotation of the coordinates. In a rotating frame that deterministic rotation disappears, so $d$ successive physical shuffles become one \emph{sweep}: one independent random swap layer in each coordinate direction. The proof then combines five ingredients. First, a collision-graph representation and negative dependence give pointwise smoothing for ordered marked cards. Second, an entropy argument is sharpened by moving an endpoint moment up to the critical exponent $\beta_c=\log_2(3/2)$, yielding an entropy-preparation clock $s^2/(2\log(3/2))+O(s\log s)$. Third, exact multiplicities in the ordered $h$-tuple permutation representation amplify marked-card bounds into Fourier operator and energy estimates on low representation levels. Fourth, entropy truncation produces a positive mixture whose regular component retains the marked-card budget. Finally, only two long blocks need this entropy regularization: a shorter third block is used solely for additional low-level smoothing. Optimizing the three block lengths gives the constant above.

papers.title: Finding non-bisimplicial and triad-free minimal separators
papers.abstract: A $u\hbox{-}v$ separator in $G$ is a set $S\subseteq V(G)\setminus\{u,v\}$ such that there is no $u\hbox{-}v$ path in $G\setminus S$. A minimal separator in $G$ is a set $S$ such that for some $u,v\in V(G)\setminus S$, $S$ is a $u\hbox{-}v$ separator in $G$ but no proper subset of $S$ is. A set $S$ is bisimplicial if it is the union of at most two cliques. Recognizing graphs in which every minimal separator is the union of at most $k$ cliques is polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We settle the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether every minimal separator in a graph is bisimplicial. A set $S$ is triad-free if its independence number $\alpha(S)$ is at most two. Given a graph $G$ and two vertices $u,v$, the problem of finding a $u\hbox{-}v$ separator $S$ with $\alpha(S)\leq k$ had the same complexity gap: it was known to be polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We resolve the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a triad-free $u\hbox{-}v$ separator or determines that none exists.

papers.title: Sparse universal graphs for planarity
papers.abstract: We show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there exists a graph $G_n$ with $(1+o(1))n$ vertices and $n^{1 + o(1)}$ edges such that every $n$-vertex planar graph is isomorphic to a subgraph of $G_n$. The best previous bound on the number of edges was $O(n^{3/2})$, proved by Babai, Chung, Erd\H{o}s, Graham, and Spencer in 1982. We then show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1 + o(1)}$ vertices and edges that contains induced copies of every $n$-vertex planar graph. This significantly reduces the number of edges in a recent construction of the authors with Dujmovi\'c, Gavoille, and Micek.

papers.title: Conjectured Bounds for 2-Local Hamiltonians via Token Graphs
papers.abstract: We explain how the maximum energy of the Quantum MaxCut, XY, and EPR Hamiltonians on a graph $G$ are related to the spectral radii of the token graphs of $G$. From numerical study, we conjecture new bounds for these spectral radii based on properties of $G$. We show how these conjectures tighten the analysis of existing algorithms, implying state-of-the-art approximation ratios for all three Hamiltonians. Our conjectures also provide simple combinatorial bounds on the ground state energy of the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, which we prove for bipartite graphs.

papers.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling
papers.abstract: We propose an algorithm to sample from composite log-concave distributions over $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e., densities of the form $\pi\propto e^{-f-g}$, assuming access to gradient evaluations of $\alpha_f$-convex $f$ and a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) for $\alpha_g$-convex $g$, where $\alpha_g \ge 0$. The latter requirement means that we can easily sample from the density $\text{RGO}_{g,h,y}(x) \propto \exp(-g(x) -\frac{1}{2h}||y-x||^2)$, which is the sampling analogue of the proximal operator for $g$. If $f + g$ is $\alpha$-convex and $f$ is $\beta$-smooth, our sampler achieves $\varepsilon$ error in total variation distance using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\kappa \sqrt d \log^4(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle calls where $\kappa := 1 \vee \beta/\alpha$, with $0\le \alpha_g \le \beta$ and $\alpha := \alpha_f + \alpha_g > 0$, which matches prior state-of-the-art results for the case $g=0$. We further extend our results to cases where (1) $\pi$ is non-log-concave but satisfies a Poincar\'e or log-Sobolev inequality, and (2) $f$ is non-smooth but Lipschitz.

papers.title: Biclique decompositions from Welzl orders
papers.abstract: A biclique decomposition of a graph is a partition of its edges into complete bipartite subgraphs. We consider graphs whose vertices can be ordered such that the neighborhood of every vertex is the union of a sublinear number of intervals. We observe that these graphs admit compact representations in the form of biclique decompositions of small size. Here, the size of a decomposition is measured as the sum of the number of vertices of its bicliques. Combining this result with the existence of suitable vertex orderings for graphs of low neighborhood complexity, as proven by Welzl in 1988, we recover and extend several known results up to logarithmic factors. These results include upper bounds on the Zarankiewicz problem, matrix multiplication, quantum circuit complexity, and shortest path algorithms in "well-structured" instances.

papers.title: The Online Steinitz Problem
papers.abstract: Inspired by Steinitz's celebrated result (1913) and recent online vector-balancing results of Kulkarni et al. (2024) and Aden-Ali (2026), we introduce the online Steinitz problem: $T$ vectors in $\mathbb R^d$, each of $\ell_2$-norm at most $1$ and with total sum zero, arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably to unused positions of an array. The goal is to keep every prefix sum of the resulting order small. We first obtain deterministic prefix-discrepancy bounds of $O(\log T)$ for $d=1$ and $O(\sqrt T)$ for $d\ge2$. Our main contribution is a general reduction that converts deterministic and randomized online vector-balancing algorithms, which assign signs to arriving vectors, into online ordering algorithms. Combined with recent vector-balancing results, this yields a randomized algorithm with prefix discrepancy $O(\log T+\sqrt{d\log T})$ and running time $O(dT\log T)$. The guarantee holds with high probability against an oblivious adversary. The reduction also gives bounds for sparse vectors and extends to inputs in arbitrary compact convex bodies. Finally, we prove matching lower bounds in both the deterministic and randomized cases.

papers.title: Approximating Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing: Analysis via Factor-Revealing LPs
papers.abstract: The capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) is one of the most extensively studied problems in combinatorial optimization. Given a depot and a set of customers with demands in a metric space, the objective is to find a set of tours, each starting and ending at the depot, operated by a capacitated vehicle located at the depot, such that all customers are served and the total travel cost is minimized. We consider the unsplittable variant, where the demand of each customer must be served entirely by a single tour. The previous best approximation ratio was about $\alpha+1.694$, where $\alpha$ is the approximation ratio for the traveling salesman problem. We propose improved approximation algorithms. First, we introduce a unified algorithmic framework that generalizes and integrates known linear programming (LP) rounding and matching-based approaches. We show that these techniques are complementary and can be combined to yield improved approximation ratios. Second, we develop a novel analytical framework based on customer demand discretization, which yields new structural bounds and, through factor-revealing LPs, achieves expected approximation ratios of about $\alpha+1.647$ for the general-capacity case and $\alpha+1.548$ for the fixed-capacity case. Finally, we derandomize our algorithms using a priori 2-tour sets and the method of conditional expectations while maintaining nearly the same approximation ratios.

papers.title: Entrywise Low-Rank Approximation and Matrix $p \rightarrow q$ Norms via Global Correlation Rounding
papers.abstract: Given a matrix $A$, the goal of the entrywise low-rank approximation problem is to find $\operatorname{argmin} \|A-B\|_p$ over all rank-$k$ matrices $B$, where $\| \cdot \|_p$ is the entrywise $\ell_p$ norm. When $p = 2$ this well-studied problem is solved by the singular value decomposition, but for $p \neq 2$ the problem becomes computationally challenging. For every even $p > 2$ and every fixed $k$, we give the first polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, improving on the $(3 + \varepsilon)$ approximation of Ban, Bhattiprolu, Bringmann, Kolev, Lee, and Woodruff, the bi-criteria approximation of Woodruff and Yasuda, and the additive approximation scheme of Anderson, Bakshi, and Hopkins. Prior algorithmic approaches based on sketching and column selection, which yielded a polynomial-time approximation scheme in the $p < 2$ setting, face concrete barriers when $p > 2$. Instead, we use the Sherali-Adams hierarchy of convex programs, and in so doing suggest a methodology for how to use convex hierarchies to design polynomial-time approximation schemes for continuous optimization problems. We use the same algorithmic strategy to give a new family of additive approximation algorithms for matrix $p \rightarrow q$ norms, which are intimately related to small-set expansion and quantum information. In particular, we give the first nontrivial additive approximation algorithms in the regime $p < 2 < q$.
